checkpoints: Nonce source is the pipeline's first stage: it mints a fresh cryptographically-random value per request and writes it to request-scoped storage — this ordering is the load-bearing contract, because a header built before minting embeds an empty nonce that matches no script.
Header builder is a pure, stateless assembly stage — the static bundle (frame/sniff/transport-security/referrer) plus the nonce plus the mode input produce the emitted headers.
Template renderer is the second consumer reading the SAME nonce from request-scoped storage and stamping it on script tags, so a single source keeps the header and the tags from ever diverging.
Report ingestion's request-handling: it accepts the report's exact content type, normalizes both wrapped/flat payload shapes, and returns 204.
Report ingestion's operational side: it logs at warn severity, extracts document-uri/violated-directive/blocked-uri for triage, and is independently deployable from the rest of the pipeline.
Mode toggle is a configuration value choosing the report-only or enforcing header name — same policy string, just an operational flip, not a code branch.
The edges: request flows into the nonce stage, which feeds both the header builder and the renderer; separately, a browser violation flows into ingestion, then into triage.
Change cases prove the boundary is right: adding a new directive touches only the builder, and adding a new nonce consumer only needs to read from that same storage, never mint its own.
Root of trust lives in the platform, never in a file; the canvas holds the platform (deployer/orchestrator), the secrets store, N service instances, an audit sink, and a rotation pipeline.

The bootstrap problem is a genuine chicken-and-egg: a freshly created service instance needs a credential to introduce itself to the secrets store, but that credential cannot arrive by living inside the image or a static config file — that would just be secret sprawl under a different name.

The fix is a split credential: every instance gets a low-secret role identifier that does nothing on its own, plus a high-secret, short-lived counterpart that the deployment platform itself injects at boot through its own identity mechanism, auto-rotated by the platform with no one managing it by hand.

The instance uses this pair to log into the secrets store in exchange for a short-lived session token carrying a lease duration (renewal must happen before the lease expires, at a cadence derived from that same lease) — and this is exactly what bounds the worth of a stolen artifact at every edge: the role identifier alone is useless without its counterpart, a stolen counterpart is only good until the platform's next rotation, and a stolen session token loses its power the moment its lease elapses.

Every secret read passes through the audit sink, and because the read cadence lands only at boot and on each refresh — not on every business request — the audit stream stays sparse enough for a human reviewer to actually read it and catch anomalies early.

The rotation pipeline has a mandatory order — write the new value to the secrets store FIRST, then trigger or await every consumer's refresh, since doing it backwards opens a window where an app holds a credential the backing system no longer accepts; the refresh interval is the upper bound on how long rotation takes to reach the whole fleet, and rotation cadence should be tiered by how sensitive/broad a credential's access is — the wider the reach, the tighter the rotation.

Failure semantics at each edge are deliberately NOT symmetric: store unreachable at boot must fail fast since an instance with no secret is useless, but store unreachable at runtime must keep serving on the cached value, log a warning, and retry rather than crash a healthy running service.

The secret never touches any persistent edge on the diagram — never written to disk, never baked into an image layer, and never relying on a child process inheriting environment as its propagation mechanism — because anywhere a secret outlives process memory is a brand-new leak surface.
Enforcing a strict CSP immediately can silently break production — inline scripts, marketing/analytics SDKs, and partner iframes can all die with no exception ever thrown.
The curated default header bundle (frame-options, nosniff, HSTS, referrer-policy, etc.) is safe to enable directly since those are sane defaults, but CSP alone needs a staged rollout.
The staged rollout starts by deploying the report-only variant carrying the intended policy plus a `/csp-report`-style endpoint, and collecting violations for 1–2 weeks.
During that collection period, separate real injection attempts from legitimate third-party sources and whitelist the legitimate ones.
Only once the report endpoint has been quiet for a day or two, flip a config flag to switch to the enforcing header.
The endpoint returns 204, logs at warn, and records document-uri/violated-directive/blocked-uri for triage.
The report-only/enforce switch must be config-driven, so graduating to enforce needs no code change and a bad enforce can be rolled back instantly.
Root cause: both incidents trace to the same underlying problem — the rate-limit key doesn't match the actual identity of the traffic.
NAT collapses many real users behind one IP, so a pure per-IP tracker mass-punishes the Hanoi office's legitimate logins as a false positive.

The credential-stuffing botnet sends only 2-3 attempts per IP across thousands of distinct IPs, staying under any per-IP threshold and never getting correlated into the single attack it actually is (false negative).

The fix is the tracker key itself, not the threshold number: switch to a composite key such as `ip:email` (or `ip:userId`) — the per-IP half still stops a single source from scanning many accounts, while the per-account half caps total attempts against any one victim no matter how many IPs the botnet routes through.
This composite key also resolves the NAT office problem, since each employee's `ip:email` pair becomes its own bucket, so one wrong password from user A doesn't touch user B's quota.
On top of the key change, add separate throttle policies per route (strict on `/auth/login`, looser on public reads) rather than one global number trying to serve both threat models.

Also layer in exponential backoff per account and/or a CAPTCHA after a handful of failures, plus monitoring the aggregate failure rate across accounts to surface the distributed botnet pattern that no single per-key counter can see.

Trap to avoid: don't turn the account-scoped limit into a hard lockout, since locking an account after N failures is DoS-by-design, letting an attacker deliberately lock out any real user by guessing wrong on purpose.
The teammate is wrong — the mistake is conflating two different classes of attack.
A CORS allowlist is a browser-enforced READ permission: it governs which origins may read a response, and says nothing about whether a request reaches the server and executes there.

A plain HTML form POST submitted from a hostile page never triggers a CORS preflight and never checks the allowlist at all, since the browser only needs permission to let JavaScript READ a response, not to SEND a request.
The browser attaches the victim's session cookies to that form submission automatically, so the request lands at the server fully authenticated — the exact CSRF vector, which CORS never even sees.

The double-submit token closes this gap: the token lives in a cookie (attached automatically) and a custom header (must be set deliberately in code), so a hostile page can force the cookie along but can't make the victim's browser set the custom header — the mismatch causes the server to reject with 403.
`SameSite=Lax` on the session cookie is a further, independent layer that withholds the cookie itself on cross-site form POSTs, closing the gap even earlier.

SameSite is not a reason to drop the token either, since it has real carve-outs (top-level GET navigations still carry the cookie) and older browsers or misconfigured attributes silently fall back to the old behavior.

Each mechanism defends a genuinely different attack: CORS protects against a hostile origin reading responses, while the CSRF token plus SameSite protect against a hostile page forging a state-changing write using the victim's session — deleting the token confuses 'nobody else can read this' with 'nobody else can make this happen,' and only defense-in-depth, not deduplication, keeps both guarantees standing.
There is no single winning algorithm — each variant trades memory, accuracy, and burst behavior differently, so a good default is a reasoned choice, not a rule of thumb.

Fixed window counts requests inside a fixed slot with O(1) memory and simplicity, but the counter resets exactly at the boundary, letting a client fire the full quota twice back-to-back across that boundary (e.g. 20 requests inside 100ms instead of the intended rate) — a bad fit for abuse-sensitive endpoints like login under credential stuffing.

Sliding window log stores every request's timestamp to count exactly how many fall in the last N seconds, giving full accuracy, but its memory cost is O(traffic) per key since every request must persist until it ages out — only viable on genuinely low-volume endpoints.

Token bucket refills N tokens at R tokens/second and spends one per request, letting legitimate bursts through smoothly up to the bucket's capacity — friendlier to real client behavior than a hard window cutoff.

Token bucket's catch is distributed correctness: the read-compute-write of checking, refilling, and decrementing tokens must happen as one atomic operation on the shared store (e.g. a single Lua `EVAL` on Redis), otherwise concurrent requests can both read a stale token count and silently double the effective limit under load.

Sliding window counter blends two adjacent fixed windows weighted by elapsed time, recovering O(1) memory per key while capping the worst-case overshoot to roughly 1.1x versus fixed window's 2x — the practical middle ground.

Sliding window counter is the reasonable company-wide default — the same one Cloudflare and Stripe run in production — because it's accurate enough, cheap enough, and doesn't require storing raw request history.

The deviation case is token bucket, reserved for endpoints where burst tolerance is a genuine product requirement (clients that batch work in short spikes); fixed window should never be the default on anything an attacker would target, like login or password-reset, precisely because its boundary flaw is a gift to credential stuffing.
Static and dynamic secrets solve two different problems, so one shouldn't be picked for everything.
A static secret is a value stored in the manager and rotated by a human or cron job — e.g. a JWT signing key, or a vendor-issued third-party API key that can't be regenerated internally.
A dynamic secret is a credential the manager mints on demand carrying a lease — e.g. a DB role that lives for one hour and then auto-revokes without anyone actively deleting it.

Dynamic reduces blast radius: a leaked credential is worth only what that one short-lived identity could do before its lease expires, and leases decay on their own without requiring detection or active revocation.
Dynamic structurally removes the rotation problem, since nothing lives long enough to need rotating — versus static's recurring rotation policy and the risk window that exists between rotations.

Dynamic isn't free: the cost is CPU spent minting credentials on demand plus integration effort, since connection pools and reconnect logic must actively cooperate with lease expiry instead of treating the credential as immutable for the connection's whole lifetime.

The realistic answer is a hybrid: use dynamic for high-impact credentials that can be rotated internally (the classic case being DB access, fully controlled by the manager), and use static for immutable, externally-issued keys with a rotation cadence tiered by access breadth (quarterly minimum, monthly for high-value, weekly for broad-access).
Regardless of static or dynamic, both still require lease-renewal discipline before expiry and per-read audit, since both flow through the same secrets manager.

The middleware's mutating-method branch has exactly one rejection condition — `headerToken !== cookieToken` — which is a strict equality comparison, not a check that a real token was ever presented; when both sides are `undefined`, `undefined !== undefined` evaluates to `false`, so the branch is skipped and `next()` runs.

A forged cross-site POST from a hostile page cannot read the victim's cookie jar (different origin) and cannot attach a custom header (a simple cross-origin form submission triggers no preflight that would carry one), so it naturally arrives with neither the CSRF cookie nor the header — exactly the equivalence class the equality check fails to reject.

Because the browser still attaches the victim's session cookie automatically on the forged request, once the flawed CSRF check falls through, the backend authenticates the request as if it came from the legitimate user.

The test suite seeds a valid cookie in every case and only varies the header value, so it only ever exercises the 'cookie present, header mismatched' branch; the both-absent case — the one that matches how a real attack actually looks — was never part of the test matrix, which is why the wrong-token tests stayed green.

Cookie minting and token verification are mixed into the same mutating-method pass: the mint block runs only when the incoming request has no cookie, but the verification step afterward re-reads `req.cookies` from that same incoming request rather than the cookie just attached to the response, so a cookie-less request still resolves `cookieToken` to `undefined`.

The core fix is to reject immediately with 403 when `!req.cookies['csrf-token']` on a mutating request, before any header comparison happens, so a missing cookie is an automatic reject rather than something that can degenerate into a passing equality check.
Cookie minting should be scoped to safe methods (GET/HEAD/OPTIONS) or a dedicated first-contact flow, and must never double as a condition that lets a mutating request skip proper verification.

Proving the fix correct requires exercising the full input matrix — both-present-matching, both-present-mismatched, header-only, cookie-only, and both-absent — plus a dedicated regression test that replays the exact forged-request shape (no cookie, no header) and asserts a 403.

NestJS runs middleware in two distinct phases: raw `app.use()` calls execute immediately, in registration order, at the Express layer, while any middleware registered through a module's `NestModule.configure()` is deferred to the later route-handler phase and only runs after every raw `app.use()` call has already fired for that request.

Helmet's `scriptSrc` callback is wired via `app.use(helmet(...))`, so it executes in the early phase and reads `res.locals.cspNonce` at that moment — before `CspNonceMiddleware`, registered through `configure()`, has had any chance to run and populate that value for the same request.

Because the nonce read happens before the nonce is minted, the read resolves to `undefined`, and the emitted `Content-Security-Policy` header ends up as `script-src 'self' 'nonce-undefined'`, a token that can never match any script tag on the page.

The rendered `<script nonce="...">` tag carries a real, correctly minted nonce because the view layer renders after the entire middleware chain — including the late-running `CspNonceMiddleware` — has finished, so the tag and the header are populated at two different points in the request lifecycle and end up out of sync.

That divergence — a real nonce on the script tag versus an empty nonce in the header — is the diagnostic signal that pins the bug to timing and ordering between two middlewares, not to a broken or misconfigured nonce generator.

Report-only mode never blocks a request regardless of policy violations, so every page load fired a CSP violation for two full weeks without any visible breakage; "quiet" only meant those violation reports were landing as unmonitored noise, not that the policy was actually compatible with the page.
Flipping `reportOnly` from `true` to `false` did not introduce a new bug — it only changed whether the browser started enforcing a policy that had already been broken from the very first request.

The fix is to register nonce minting as a raw `app.use()` call in the same early Express-layer phase as Helmet, and to order it strictly before Helmet's registration, rather than through `NestModule.configure()`, which structurally fires too late to affect a header already built at request time.

Correctness should be proven with a per-response assertion that the nonce embedded in the `Content-Security-Policy` header string equals the nonce present on the rendered `<script>` tag, followed by re-running the report-only-to-enforce flip in staging and confirming the violation stream stays quiet — and confirming that violation-reporting endpoint actually feeds a dashboard someone owns, so a future graduation to enforce mode cannot go unmonitored the same way again.

Reading the client IP from the first entry of `x-forwarded-for` without validating a trusted-proxy hop count treats an attacker-controlled header as ground truth: an attacker can send a different fabricated value on every request, so each request lands in a fresh rate-limit bucket and the counter never accumulates past 1 — a complete bypass rather than a partial weakening.

The correct fix for header-based client IP is configuring the trusted proxy chain to the actual hop count (for example `app.set('trust proxy', <hopCount>)`), so the framework strips client-injected entries and keeps only the value appended by the trusted load balancer.

Falling back to a per-process in-memory Map and returning true whenever the Redis-backed counter throws is a fail-open design for a security control: it turns a Redis outage into every replica running its own private, unshared counter, silently multiplying the effective rate limit by replica count and going dark exactly when it's needed most.

An abuse control like a login rate limiter must fail closed on a counter-store error — rejecting the request during an outage costs some availability, but a control that silently opens exactly when a distributed brute-force attack is most likely to be running is worse than no control at all.

Setting `user.locked = true` permanently once failed-login count reaches a threshold, with no code path anywhere to clear it, converts the lockout mechanism into a weapon: anyone who knows a victim's email can lock that account on purpose with five wrong passwords, forcing a support ticket to recover.

A safer response to repeated failed logins is exponential backoff per account combined with a CAPTCHA challenge after repeated failures, since this keeps raising the attacker's cost without ever handing an anonymous requester a permanent-lockout button against someone else's account.

Verifying a fix like this needs adversarial tests, not a single manual check from one tester: a request series rotating a forged `x-forwarded-for` value on every call must still return 429 by the expected attempt, a chaos test with the counter store stopped must show the request rejected rather than admitted, and repeated wrong-password attempts must show growing delay or a CAPTCHA challenge rather than a permanent lock.

Prioritizing PR findings by exploitability rather than by code style separates two complete bypasses — the spoofable rate-limit key and the fail-open counter fallback — from a design flaw with user-facing harm — the permanent lockout — with attacker impact, not stylistic preference, deciding what blocks approval.
